Pressure Measurement

 Pressure Gauge Accuracy Classes Explained: 8 Reliable ASME B40.100 Grades to Avoid Costly Mistakes

 Two gauges can look identical on the shelf and still disagree by 5% of span at the same reading, purely because they carry different ASME accuracy grades. Knowing what those grade letters actually mean is what keeps a spec sheet honest.

 
 Full ASME B40.100 Table 
 Live Accuracy Calculator 
 4A to D Explained 
 




 Pressure gauge accuracy classes under ASME B40.100 define exactly how much error a gauge is allowed, as a percent of its full span, so engineers can compare gauges from different manufacturers on equal terms.


 Every dial pressure gauge sold for industrial use carries an accuracy grade somewhere on its dial or datasheet, usually written as a letter and number like 2A, 1A, or B. That grade isn't a marketing label. It's a defined tolerance from ASME B40.100 , the American standard that governs dial and digital pressure gauges, and it tells you precisely how far a reading is allowed to drift from the true pressure.


 
 
 

 Get the accuracy class wrong on a specification and one of two things happens. Either the plant pays for a far more precise gauge than the process ever needed, or a critical measurement ends up relying on a gauge that was never built to hold the tolerance the application actually requires. Both mistakes are avoidable once the eight ASME B40.100 grades are actually understood.

 Why Pressure Gauge Accuracy Classes Exist

 Before ASME formalized these grades, two manufacturers could both call a gauge "accurate" while meaning completely different things by it. One might be quoting error at mid scale only, another might be quoting the worst case anywhere on the dial, and a buyer had no simple way to compare them side by side.

 ASME B40.100 fixes that by forcing every accuracy claim into one of eight standardized boxes. Once a gauge is stamped Grade 2A, that number means exactly the same thing whether the gauge came from a large multinational manufacturer or a small regional shop, because both were tested against the same permissible error table.

 This matters most during calibration and audits. An instrument technician checking a gauge against a certified reference standard needs to know the pass or fail tolerance before running the test, and the accuracy grade printed on the dial is exactly that tolerance, already defined by the standard rather than left to interpretation.


 The 8 ASME B40.100 Pressure Gauge Accuracy Classes

 ASME B40.100 defines exactly eight accuracy grades, running from the tightest tolerance down to the loosest. Here they are in order, from most to least accurate.


 
 
 1

 Grade 4A: ±0.1% of span
 The tightest ASME grade, reserved for laboratory standards and primary calibration references. Needs an 8.5 inch or larger dial.


 

 
 2

 Grade 3A: ±0.25% of span
 Used for high precision test gauges and master reference instruments. Minimum dial size is 4.5 inches.


 

 
 3

 Grade 2A: ±0.5% of span
 The most common accuracy for 4.5 inch process gauges on critical process measurements. Minimum dial size is 2.5 inches.


 

 
 4

 Grade 1A: ±1.0% of span
 A common general industrial process accuracy, balancing cost and precision. Minimum dial size is 1.5 inches.


 

 
 5

 Grade A: 2-1-2% of span
 Error is defined in three zones: 2% in the lower quarter, 1% in the middle half, 2% in the upper quarter. Common on utility and commercial gauges.


 

 
 6

 Grade B: 3-2-3% of span
 A looser three zone tolerance, typical of economy commercial and residential pressure gauges.


 

 
 7

 Grade C: 4-3-4% of span
 Used on basic utility gauges where precise readings aren't critical to the application.


 

 
 8

 Grade D: 5-5-5% of span
 The loosest ASME grade, a flat 5% error across the entire span, suited only to rough visual indication.


 




 Two Ways ASME B40.100 Defines Error

 The eight pressure gauge accuracy classes actually split into two different definitions of error, and mixing them up is a common specification mistake.


 
 
 🎯

 Grades 4A Through 1A: Single Value

 Error is defined as one flat percentage of span across the entire scale, excluding friction. A 2A gauge is within 0.5% of span everywhere on the dial.

 Simple, uniform tolerance

 

 
 📊

 Grades A Through D: Three Zones

 Error is allowed to be looser at the low and high ends of the dial and tightest in the middle half, written as three numbers like 3-2-3%.

 Zone-based tolerance

 




 
 
 Image credit: Ashcroft Inc., ASME B40.100 accuracy chart 
 

 
 A gauge marked "2A" is not automatically better than one marked "B" everywhere on the dial. Near the low end of the scale, a 2A gauge's flat 0.5% can occasionally read looser in absolute terms than expected if the span is very wide, so always compare error in actual engineering units, not just the grade letter.

 Practical specification tip

 Percent of Span Formula and Worked Example

 Every ASME B40.100 grade is expressed as a percent of span, and converting that percentage into real engineering units is simple once you know the gauge's full scale range.


 
 Permissible Error Formula

 Allowable Error = (Grade % / 100) x Full Scale Span

 
 Example: 4.5 inch gauge, Grade 2A, full scale range = 0 to 300 psi

 Full Scale Span = 300 psi

 Allowable Error = (0.5 / 100) x 300 psi

 Allowable Error = 1.5 psi


 Meaning: at any point on the dial, this gauge's reading can be off by up to 1.5 psi and still meet its 2A rating.
